overview: A dbt project is a structured folder of files - SQL models, YAML configuration, seeds, macros, tests, and snapshots - governed by a single dbt_project.yml file that tells dbt how everything is organized and how models should be materialized.

Connection details live separately in profiles.yml, which stores warehouse credentials and one or more targets (e.g., dev and prod), so the same project code can run against different environments and warehouses without any change to the SQL.

The convention-driven layout (models split into staging, intermediate, and marts; plus seeds/, macros/, tests/, snapshots/, analyses/) and reproducible compiled artifacts in target/ (manifest.json, run_results.json) are what make dbt projects consistent, portable, and collaborative across a team.
learningObjectives: Scaffold a dbt project with dbt init and describe the role of every top-level folder and configuration file.
Explain the separation between dbt_project.yml (project config, in git) and profiles.yml (connection secrets, not in git) and why it matters.
Configure materializations by folder, install packages with packages.yml + dbt deps, and interpret the compiled artifacts dbt writes to the target/ directory.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A dbt project is a directory tree whose entry point is dbt_project.yml, a YAML file declaring the project name, the profile it uses, and configuration such as model/seed/test paths and folder-scoped materializations. Model SQL, YAML property files, seeds, macros, tests, snapshots, and analyses are organized into conventional subdirectories. A separate profiles.yml defines connection profiles and their targets (host, warehouse, schema, threads, credentials) that the adapter uses to connect. Third-party code is declared in packages.yml and fetched with dbt deps. On each invocation dbt compiles the project into the target/ directory, emitting artifacts including manifest.json (the full parsed graph) and run_results.json (execution outcomes).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of a dbt project like a well-organized cookbook. dbt_project.yml is the cover page and table of contents - it names the book and tells you how the chapters (folders) are laid out and how each type of dish should be prepared by default. The models/ folder holds your recipes, split into prep work (staging), sub-assemblies (intermediate), and finished dishes (marts). profiles.yml is kept separately, like the key to the kitchen and pantry - it holds the secret credentials to actually get into the warehouse, so you never print those secrets inside the shared cookbook. packages.yml is a shopping list of other people's recipe books (like dbt_utils) that you pull in with dbt deps. Every time dbt runs, it writes its 'compiled notes' into a target/ scratchpad so it knows exactly what it built and in what order.
coreConcept.historicalContext: When dbt Labs (then Fishtown Analytics) built dbt around 2016, they deliberately borrowed conventions from software projects: a manifest-style config file (dbt_project.yml), a clear directory layout, and dependency management, so analytics code could be version-controlled and shared like application code. The profiles.yml separation was designed from the start to keep warehouse secrets out of the git repo. As the ecosystem matured, dbt Labs published the widely adopted 'staging -> intermediate -> marts' structuring guide, and the dbt Package Hub (with packages like dbt_utils) standardized reusable macros. The compiled artifacts in target/ (especially manifest.json) later became the foundation for state-based selection, docs, and metadata tooling across the data ecosystem.

whyItMatters.business: A consistent, documented project structure means new analysts become productive quickly and the transformation codebase remains understandable as the team and the number of datasets grow, protecting the business's investment in its analytics.
whyItMatters.engineering: Separating configuration (dbt_project.yml, in git) from secrets (profiles.yml, outside git) is a security and portability best practice; folder-scoped materialization config removes repetitive boilerplate and enforces conventions automatically.
whyItMatters.scalability: Conventional layering (staging/intermediate/marts) and reusable packages keep a project maintainable as it scales from tens to thousands of models, because responsibilities are clear and shared logic is not copy-pasted.
whyItMatters.cost: Setting sensible default materializations per folder (cheap views for staging, tables for reused marts) directly controls warehouse spend without editing every model, and packages avoid re-implementing (and re-paying to debug) common logic.
whyItMatters.reliability: Reproducible compiled artifacts (manifest.json, run_results.json) and a deterministic project structure make builds predictable and debuggable, and a correct profiles.yml with distinct dev/prod targets prevents accidents like writing to production from a laptop.

coreComponents.name: dbt_project.yml
coreComponents.definition: The mandatory root configuration file that names the project, points to the profile to use, and declares path settings and folder-scoped configuration such as default materializations.
coreComponents.purpose: To be the single source of truth for how the project is organized and how models are built by default, versioned in git alongside the code.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Declare name/profile/version, set model-paths/seed-paths/etc., and configure materialization and other settings per folder under the models: key.

coreComponents.name: profiles.yml
coreComponents.definition: A separate YAML file (by default in ~/.dbt/) that stores connection profiles, each with one or more targets (dev, prod) holding warehouse type, account/host, schema, threads, and credentials.
coreComponents.purpose: To hold environment-specific connection details and secrets outside the git repo, so the same project runs anywhere by selecting a target.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Define the warehouse adapter and credentials, set threads for parallelism, and map logical target names (dev/prod) to concrete connections.
coreComponents.examples: target: dev | outputs: dev: {type: snowflake, account: ..., schema: dbt_dev, threads: 4}

coreComponents.name: Project folders and packages
coreComponents.definition: Conventional subdirectories - models/ (staging, intermediate, marts), seeds/, macros/, tests/, snapshots/, analyses/ - plus packages.yml declaring third-party packages installed by dbt deps.
coreComponents.purpose: To organize each kind of artifact by responsibility and to reuse community code (e.g., dbt_utils) instead of re-writing it.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Hold models/tests/macros/etc. in predictable locations, and manage external dependencies fetched into dbt_packages/.

internalWorking: When you run any dbt command, dbt reads dbt_project.yml to learn the project name and which profile to use, then loads that profile from profiles.yml to get the connection target (and credentials) for the environment you selected with --target.

dbt walks the configured paths (model-paths, seed-paths, macro-paths, etc.), parsing every .sql and .yml file and merging folder-scoped configuration from dbt_project.yml with in-file config() blocks, where the more specific config wins.
For third-party code, dbt reads packages.yml and, when you run dbt deps, downloads each package into the dbt_packages/ directory so its models and macros become available to your project.

dbt then builds the full parsed graph and writes it to target/manifest.json, along with compiled SQL for each model under target/compiled/ and target/run/ - the exact CREATE statements it will send to the warehouse.

After executing, dbt records the outcome of every node (success, error, timing, rows) in target/run_results.json, which downstream tooling and state-based selection (--select state:modified+) use to know what changed and what happened.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: dbt init (scaffold) -> dbt_project.yml (names project + selects profile) -> profiles.yml (resolves target + credentials) -> dbt deps (installs packages.yml into dbt_packages/) -> parse folders (models/seeds/macros/...) + merge config -> compile to target/ (manifest.json, compiled SQL) -> execute against warehouse -> run_results.json
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You run 'dbt init analytics', which scaffolds the folder structure and dbt_project.yml and prompts you to create a profiles.yml entry for your warehouse.
2. dbt_project.yml sets name: 'analytics' and profile: 'analytics', and configures models: staging: +materialized: view and marts: +materialized: table.
3. On 'dbt run', dbt loads the 'analytics' profile from profiles.yml, picks the dev target, and connects to the warehouse with those credentials and thread count.
4. dbt parses models/staging/*.sql and models/marts/*.sql, applying the folder-scoped materializations (staging as views, marts as tables) unless a model overrides it with its own config().
5. dbt compiles everything into target/ (manifest.json + compiled SQL), executes the CREATE statements in DAG order against the dev schema, and writes results to target/run_results.json.

keyTerminology.meaning: A profile is a named set of connection outputs in profiles.yml; a target (e.g., dev, prod) is one specific connection within that profile chosen at run time.
keyTerminology.importance: The profile/target split is how one project safely runs in multiple environments; selecting the wrong target is how people accidentally write to production.

keyTerminology.meaning: Configuration set under the models: key in dbt_project.yml that applies to all models in a folder (e.g., +materialized: view for staging).
keyTerminology.importance: It removes repetitive config() blocks and enforces conventions project-wide, and it is overridden by more specific in-file config.

keyTerminology.meaning: Reusable dbt code (macros, models, tests) from the dbt Package Hub or git, declared in packages.yml and installed into dbt_packages/ by dbt deps.
keyTerminology.importance: Packages like dbt_utils save you from re-implementing common SQL patterns and are a standard part of professional dbt setups.

keyTerminology.meaning: Files dbt writes when it compiles and runs: manifest.json is the full parsed graph; run_results.json records execution outcomes and timing.
keyTerminology.importance: These artifacts power docs, lineage, state-based selection, and monitoring, and should be gitignored because they are generated output.

importantConcepts.concept: Why profiles.yml is separate from the project
importantConcepts.explanation: What: connection details and credentials live in profiles.yml (by default in ~/.dbt/), completely outside the git-tracked project. Why: secrets must never be committed to version control, and different developers and environments need different connections without editing shared code. How: dbt_project.yml only names a profile; dbt resolves it against profiles.yml at run time, choosing a target like dev or prod. Pitfall: hard-coding credentials in dbt_project.yml or committing profiles.yml leaks secrets; the correct pattern is environment variables (via env_var) for CI/prod and a local, untracked profiles.yml for development.

What: instead of repeating config(materialized=...) in every model, you set defaults per folder under the models: key in dbt_project.yml. Why: it keeps conventions consistent (all staging = views, all marts = tables) and reduces boilerplate as the project grows. How: 'models: analytics: staging: +materialized: view' applies to every model in models/staging/; the leading + marks a config key. Pitfall: forgetting that an in-file config() block always overrides the folder default, so a stray config() can silently change how one model materializes regardless of the project-level setting.

What: dbt Labs' recommended way to organize models/ into layers by purpose. Why: it gives every model a clear role and keeps them small and composable. How: staging models (stg_) do one-to-one light cleaning of each source (usually views); intermediate models (int_) hold reusable joins/logic that are not final; marts (fct_/dim_) are the business-ready outputs (often tables). Pitfall: skipping the layers and writing giant models that read straight from sources and do everything at once, which destroys reusability and makes lineage unreadable.

variationsAndTypes: **Top-level folders:** models/ (transformations), seeds/ (small CSVs loaded as tables), macros/ (reusable Jinja/SQL), tests/ (singular data tests), snapshots/ (slowly changing dimension captures), analyses/ (ad-hoc SQL that is compiled but not run).
**Model layers:** staging/ (stg_, one per source, light cleanup), intermediate/ (int_, reusable mid-logic), marts/ (fct_/dim_, business-ready outputs).
**Profile targets:** dev (a personal/dev schema, low threads) vs prod (the production schema/role, often higher threads), selected with --target.
**Config placement:** folder-scoped config in dbt_project.yml vs per-model config() blocks vs YAML property-file config - most specific wins.
**Package sources:** dbt Package Hub (dbt-labs/dbt_utils), git repositories, and local packages, all declared in packages.yml and installed by dbt deps.
advantages: **Convention over configuration:** a scaffolded, well-known layout means any dbt developer instantly understands where things live and how models build.
**Environment portability:** the profile/target design lets the same code run in dev, CI, and prod just by switching targets, with no SQL changes.
**Less boilerplate:** folder-scoped materialization config sets sensible defaults once instead of repeating config() in every model.
**Reuse via packages:** packages.yml + dbt deps pull in battle-tested community code (dbt_utils, etc.), avoiding reinventing common patterns.
disadvantages: **Setup learning curve:** newcomers must learn the difference between dbt_project.yml and profiles.yml and where each lives, which is a common early stumbling block.
**Config precedence confusion:** folder vs file vs YAML config precedence can surprise people, causing models to materialize differently than expected.
**Secret management effort:** keeping profiles.yml out of git and injecting env vars in CI/prod requires deliberate setup and discipline.
**Structure overhead for tiny projects:** the full staging/intermediate/marts layout can feel heavy for a handful of models, though it pays off as the project grows.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Adopt the full conventional structure (layered models, packages, per-folder config, distinct dev/prod targets) for any team project or one expected to grow, because the consistency and safety pay off quickly.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: For a throwaway or single-analyst proof of concept you can start with a minimal structure, but avoid committing profiles.yml or hard-coding credentials even then, and avoid collapsing everything into one folder if the project is likely to outlive the prototype.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Setting up a dbt project is like organizing a professional kitchen before service. dbt_project.yml is the operations manual posted on the wall: it names the restaurant, says which supplier account to use, and states the house rules (staging dishes are always plated as light 'views', signature dishes as full 'tables'). profiles.yml is the manager's private keyring - the codes to the pantry and walk-in - kept off the public manual so no one can copy your supplier credentials. The stations (folders) are labeled clearly: prep (staging), sub-assembly (intermediate), and the pass where finished plates go out (marts). packages.yml is your standing order of pre-made staples (like dbt_utils stock) delivered by dbt deps. And target/ is the expo's ticket rail, recording exactly what was fired and how it turned out.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Connection credentials belong in dbt_project.yml along with the rest of the config.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Credentials belong in profiles.yml (outside the git repo) or in environment variables. dbt_project.yml only references a profile by name; keeping secrets out of the versioned project is a core dbt design principle.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The target/ folder is source code you should commit and edit.
commonMisconceptions.reality: target/ (and dbt_packages/) are generated output - compiled SQL, manifest.json, run_results.json. They are recreated on every run, should be gitignored, and are never edited by hand.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must set materialization in every model's config() block.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You can set defaults per folder in dbt_project.yml (e.g., +materialized: view for staging), and only override in individual models when needed; the folder-scoped config handles the common case with no per-model boilerplate.

productionConsiderations.scalability: As models grow into the hundreds or thousands, lean on the layered folder structure and folder-scoped config to keep things organized, and raise the threads setting in the prod target so dbt parallelizes independent models across the DAG.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Maintain distinct dev and prod targets with different schemas and roles so development can never overwrite production; pin package versions in packages.yml so builds are reproducible and dbt deps installs the same code every time.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because manifest.json and run_results.json capture exact graph and outcomes, you can rerun only failed or changed nodes with selectors; a well-structured project makes it easy to isolate and rebuild a single failing area.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Ship target/run_results.json (per-node timing and status) and manifest.json to your observability stack after each run to track build durations, failures, and model counts over time.
productionConsiderations.security: Never commit profiles.yml or credentials; use env_var() to inject secrets from a secrets manager in CI/prod, and scope the prod target's warehouse role to only the schemas the project manages.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Set folder-level defaults so staging stays as cheap views and only reused marts become tables, and tune the target's warehouse size/threads so parallelism matches the compute you are paying for.
productionConsiderations.performance: Increase threads in profiles.yml to run more independent models concurrently, keep dbt_packages/ installed via dbt deps in CI so parsing is fast, and rely on state comparison against a prior manifest.json to build only what changed.

codeExamples.title: dbt_project.yml: naming the project and configuring materializations by folder
codeExamples.overview: The root config file that names the project, points to a profile, sets the standard paths, and defines default materializations for the staging and marts layers.
codeExamples.code:
# dbt_project.yml  (lives at the project root, tracked in git)
name: 'analytics'
version: '1.0.0'
config-version: 2

# Which profile in profiles.yml to use for the warehouse connection
profile: 'analytics'

# Where dbt looks for each kind of file (these are the defaults)
model-paths: ["models"]
seed-paths: ["seeds"]
macro-paths: ["macros"]
test-paths: ["tests"]
snapshot-paths: ["snapshots"]
analysis-paths: ["analyses"]

# Generated output - safe to delete, should be gitignored
target-path: "target"
clean-targets: ["target", "dbt_packages"]

# Folder-scoped configuration: set defaults per model layer
models:
  analytics:            # must match the 'name' above
    staging:
      +materialized: view     # staging models are cheap, always-fresh views
    intermediate:
      +materialized: ephemeral
    marts:
      +materialized: table    # marts are reused, so build as tables
codeExamples.breakdown: name and profile are required: name identifies the project and must match the top key under models:, while profile tells dbt which entry in profiles.yml to connect with. The *-paths keys point dbt at each folder (shown here as the defaults). The models: block applies folder-scoped config: every model in models/staging/ becomes a view, intermediate becomes ephemeral, and marts becomes a table - the leading + marks a config key. clean-targets lists directories that 'dbt clean' can wipe.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: With this file in place, 'dbt run' materializes staging models as views and mart models as tables automatically, with no config() block needed in the individual SQL files unless you want to override the folder default.
codeExamples.commonIssues: The nested key under models: must exactly equal the project name ('analytics' here); a mismatch means the config is silently ignored. Omitting config-version: 2 or profile causes dbt to error on startup.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep staging as views and only promote heavy, reused marts to tables; use ephemeral for intermediate models so they are inlined and never create a warehouse object you have to pay to store.

codeExamples.title: profiles.yml: dev and prod targets for a Snowflake warehouse
codeExamples.overview: The connection file (kept outside git in ~/.dbt/profiles.yml) that defines two targets - a personal dev schema and a production schema - using environment variables for secrets.
codeExamples.code:
# ~/.dbt/profiles.yml  (NOT in the git repo)
analytics:                 # must match 'profile' in dbt_project.yml
  target: dev              # the default target if --target is not passed
  outputs:
    dev:
      type: snowflake
      account: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT') }}"
      user: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_USER') }}"
      password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') }}"
      role: TRANSFORMER
      warehouse: DEV_WH
      database: ANALYTICS_DB
      schema: dbt_dev       # personal dev schema, safe to rebuild
      threads: 4
    prod:
      type: snowflake
      account: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT') }}"
      user: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PROD_USER') }}"
      password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PROD_PASSWORD') }}"
      role: TRANSFORMER_PROD
      warehouse: PROD_WH
      database: ANALYTICS_DB
      schema: analytics     # the shared production schema
      threads: 8
codeExamples.breakdown: The top key 'analytics' matches the profile named in dbt_project.yml. target: dev is the default environment used when you do not pass --target. Each entry under outputs is a target: dev writes to a personal dbt_dev schema with 4 threads, while prod writes to the shared analytics schema with 8 threads and a stricter role. env_var() injects secrets at run time so no passwords are ever written into the file or git. threads controls how many models dbt builds in parallel.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: 'dbt run' uses the dev target (writing to dbt_dev), while 'dbt run --target prod' uses the prod target (writing to analytics) - the same model code, two isolated environments.
codeExamples.commonIssues: A mismatch between the profile name here and in dbt_project.yml gives 'Could not find profile named ...'. Forgetting to export the referenced env vars causes an env_var error at parse time. Committing this file leaks credentials.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Raise threads on prod to increase parallelism up to the warehouse's capacity, keep dev on a small warehouse to save money, and always source secrets from env vars or a secrets manager rather than plaintext.

codeExamples.title: Scaffolding, installing packages, and inspecting artifacts (CLI + packages.yml)
codeExamples.overview: The end-to-end setup workflow: initialize a project, declare and install dbt_utils, verify the connection, and build - then look at what lands in target/.
codeExamples.code:
# 1. Scaffold a brand-new project (creates folders + dbt_project.yml,
#    and prompts you to set up a profiles.yml connection)
dbt init analytics

# 2. Declare a package dependency in packages.yml:
#    ---------------------------------------------
#    packages:
#      - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
#        version: 1.3.0
#    ---------------------------------------------

# 3. Install packages into the dbt_packages/ directory
dbt deps

# 4. Verify the warehouse connection defined in profiles.yml
dbt debug

# 5. Compile SQL only (writes to target/ without touching the warehouse)
dbt compile

# 6. Build all models + tests, then look at the generated artifacts
dbt build
ls target/          # -> manifest.json  run_results.json  compiled/  run/
codeExamples.breakdown: dbt init scaffolds the whole project layout and dbt_project.yml. packages.yml declares dbt_utils (a widely used macro package), and dbt deps downloads it into dbt_packages/. dbt debug confirms credentials and connectivity before you run anything. dbt compile resolves Jinja and writes compiled SQL into target/ without executing it. dbt build then runs models and tests; afterward target/ holds manifest.json (the full parsed graph), run_results.json (per-node outcomes), and the compiled/ and run/ SQL folders.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
dbt deps:
15:20:01  Installing dbt-labs/dbt_utils
15:20:02  Installed from version 1.3.0

dbt debug:
15:20:10  Connection test: [OK connection ok]
15:20:10  All checks passed!

dbt build:
15:21:00  Found 5 models, 8 tests, 1 seed, 3 sources
15:21:05  Completed successfully
15:21:05  Done. PASS=13 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=13
codeExamples.commonIssues: Running dbt without first running dbt deps causes 'macro dbt_utils... not found'. Committing target/ or dbt_packages/ bloats the repo - both should be gitignored. Skipping dbt debug means connection problems only surface later during dbt run.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pin package versions in packages.yml for reproducible builds; run dbt deps in CI before dbt build; use dbt compile to preview the exact SQL a model produces before running it against the warehouse.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A startup's single analyst has grown into a three-person analytics team. Their transformation SQL lives in scattered scripts with hard-coded credentials, and everyone writes to the same production schema, causing accidental overwrites. They need a properly structured, shareable dbt project with safe dev and prod environments.
endToEndExample.inputData: Raw tables already loaded into Snowflake by Fivetran (raw.orders, raw.customers, raw.products), plus a small reference CSV of country codes the team maintains by hand.
endToEndExample.architecture: A git-tracked dbt project with dbt_project.yml (name 'analytics', profile 'analytics', folder-scoped materializations), a local profiles.yml with dev/prod Snowflake targets using env vars, models split into staging/intermediate/marts, the country codes as a seed, and dbt_utils installed via packages.yml.
processingSteps: 1. Run 'dbt init analytics' to scaffold the project, then commit dbt_project.yml and the folder structure to git.
2. Create ~/.dbt/profiles.yml with dev (schema dbt_dev) and prod (schema analytics) targets, sourcing Snowflake credentials from environment variables so nothing secret enters git.
3. Add packages.yml declaring dbt-labs/dbt_utils and run 'dbt deps' to install it into dbt_packages/; place country_codes.csv in seeds/.

4. Organize models: models/staging/ (stg_orders, stg_customers as views), models/intermediate/ (int_orders_enriched, ephemeral), models/marts/ (fct_orders as a table), with materializations set per folder in dbt_project.yml.

5. Each analyst runs 'dbt build' (defaulting to their dev schema); the CI pipeline runs 'dbt build --target prod' to publish, and everyone inspects target/run_results.json for timings and test results.
endToEndExample.output: A version-controlled dbt project where every developer safely builds into an isolated dbt_dev schema, production is published only through CI to the analytics schema, common logic comes from dbt_utils, and each run produces reproducible artifacts in target/.
endToEndExample.monitoring: run_results.json from each build is captured to track per-model timing and test pass/fail; dbt debug is part of CI to catch connection issues early; source freshness and the model count from manifest.json are tracked as the project grows.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Distinct dev/prod targets mean a mistake in development can never overwrite production; if dbt deps or dbt debug fails, the build stops before any warehouse changes; a failed test in dbt build errors the model and skips its dependents.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The team collaborates on one clean, structured codebase: credentials are safe in profiles.yml/env vars, dev and prod are isolated, reusable logic is installed via packages, and the whole project is reproducible and reviewable - eliminating the accidental-overwrite and scattered-script problems.

industryUseCases.company: Early-stage startups scaling their first data team
industryUseCases.problem: A lone analyst's ad-hoc SQL scripts with embedded credentials do not survive the team growing to several people who need to work safely in parallel.
industryUseCases.solution: Adopt a scaffolded dbt project with dbt_project.yml in git, a per-developer profiles.yml with dev/prod targets, and the standard layered folder structure.
industryUseCases.benefits: Safe parallel development in isolated dev schemas, no secrets in git, and a codebase new hires can understand immediately.

industryUseCases.problem: Dozens of teams each structured their dbt projects differently, making shared tooling, onboarding, and governance painful.
industryUseCases.solution: Enforce a common project template (dbt_project.yml conventions, folder layout, packages.yml with an internal utils package) across all teams.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent structure everywhere, reusable internal packages, and centralized metadata via each project's manifest.json artifacts.

industryUseCases.problem: Consultants must hand off portable projects that clients can run in their own warehouses without exposing credentials.
industryUseCases.solution: Ship a git repo with dbt_project.yml and env-var-based profiles.yml templates, plus pinned packages, so clients supply only their own connection details.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fully portable, secret-free deliverables that run in any environment simply by populating the client's profiles.yml target.

productionDeepDive.scalability: The layered folder structure plus folder-scoped config keeps large projects (thousands of models) organized without per-model boilerplate, and raising threads in the prod target lets dbt exploit DAG parallelism as model count grows.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: manifest.json and run_results.json record the exact graph and each node's outcome, so failed or changed nodes can be selectively rerun (e.g., --select state:modified+) rather than rebuilding everything after a partial failure.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: The project itself is stateless code plus config; availability rests on the managed warehouse and the CI/orchestrator, and any runner with the repo, dbt deps installed, and valid credentials can execute the same build.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because dbt_project.yml, models, and packages.yml are all in git and raw sources are immutable, the entire transformed layer can be rebuilt from scratch by cloning the repo, running dbt deps, and running dbt build against retained raw data.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Tune threads per target to match warehouse capacity, install packages once in CI so parsing is fast, and use state comparison against a stored manifest.json so only modified models are compiled and built.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Set folder-level defaults so staging stays as cheap views and only reused marts become tables, keep dev on a small warehouse, and use ephemeral for intermediate models so they create no billable warehouse objects.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Keep profiles.yml and all credentials out of git, inject secrets via env_var() from a secrets manager in CI/prod, and scope each target's role to the minimum schemas it needs so dev cannot touch production data.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Capture run_results.json (timings, statuses) and manifest.json (graph, model counts) after each run and feed them to dashboards to watch build health, slow models, and project growth over time.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Because tests live in the versioned project and dbt build runs them by default, quality checks are reproducible; source freshness config in the source YAML catches stale raw data before models build.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: dbt writes structured logs plus run_results.json for every invocation; wire CI/orchestrator alerts to build failures, dbt debug failures, and package-install errors so setup and connection problems are caught immediately.

recommendedPractices: **Keep profiles.yml out of git** and source all credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager, never hard-coded in the project.
**Use distinct dev and prod targets** with different schemas and roles so development can never overwrite production.
**Set materializations at the folder level** in dbt_project.yml (views for staging, tables for marts) instead of repeating config() in every model.
**Pin package versions in packages.yml** and run dbt deps before every build so dependencies are reproducible.
engineeringStandards: Gitignore target/ and dbt_packages/ because they are generated output, not source code.
Ensure the nested key under models: in dbt_project.yml exactly matches the project name so folder config actually applies.
Run dbt debug in CI as a first step to fail fast on connection or profile misconfiguration.
designRecommendations: Organize models into staging/ (stg_), intermediate/ (int_), and marts/ (fct_/dim_) so each model has one clear responsibility.
Put small, hand-maintained reference data in seeds/ rather than hard-coding it into models.
Extract repeated SQL logic into macros/ or pull it from a package like dbt_utils instead of copy-pasting.
namingConventions: Give the project a clear name in dbt_project.yml and reuse it as the top key under models: and as the profile name for consistency.
Name profiles.yml targets by environment (dev, prod, ci) so the intent of each connection is obvious.
Prefix models by layer (stg_, int_, fct_/dim_) so the folder and the file name tell the same story.
documentationStandards: Document in the repo README how to create the local profiles.yml and which env vars are required.
Comment non-obvious folder-scoped config in dbt_project.yml so future maintainers understand the materialization choices.
Record pinned package versions and why they were chosen alongside packages.yml.
testingStrategies: Run dbt debug and dbt deps in CI before dbt build to validate setup and dependencies.
Build into an ephemeral CI schema (a separate target) so tests never touch dev or prod data.
Verify that folder-scoped materializations produce the expected object types (views vs tables) by inspecting the warehouse after a first run.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing profiles.yml or hard-coding warehouse credentials in the project.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the quickest way to get a connection working, and beginners do not realize profiles.yml lives outside the repo by design.
commonMistakes.impact: Leaked credentials in git history, a serious security incident that is hard to fully remediate, and non-portable projects tied to one person's setup.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Keep profiles.yml in ~/.dbt/ (outside git), reference secrets with env_var(), and document the required environment variables in the README.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mismatching the project name between the 'name' key and the nested key under 'models:' in dbt_project.yml.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The two must be identical, but people rename the project in one place and forget the other, and dbt does not loudly complain.
commonMistakes.impact: Folder-scoped materialization config is silently ignored, so models build with the wrong materialization (often defaulting to view) without any error.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use the exact project name as both the 'name' value and the top key under 'models:', and verify by checking that a first run produces the intended object types.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing the target/ and dbt_packages/ directories to git.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: They appear after the first run and look like part of the project, so people add them without realizing they are generated output.
commonMistakes.impact: Bloated repositories, noisy diffs on every run, and merge conflicts on compiled artifacts that provide no real value.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add target/ and dbt_packages/ to .gitignore; regenerate them anytime with dbt deps and dbt compile/build.

comparisonSection.explanation: dbt_project.yml lives in the git repo and configures the project itself - its name, the profile to use, path settings, and folder-scoped model config like materializations. profiles.yml lives outside the repo (by default ~/.dbt/) and holds the actual warehouse connection: adapter type, account/host, schema, threads, and credentials, organized into targets like dev and prod. The split exists so shared project config is versioned while environment-specific secrets stay private and swappable.

Folder-scoped config in dbt_project.yml sets a default for every model in a folder (e.g., +materialized: view for staging), which is concise and enforces conventions project-wide. A per-model config() block sets materialization for one specific model and always overrides the folder default. Use folder config for the common case and reserve in-file config() for the exceptions; remember the most specific setting always wins, which is a frequent source of surprise.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between dbt_project.yml and profiles.yml?
beginnerQuestions.answer: dbt_project.yml is the project's configuration file, tracked in git, that names the project, points to a profile, sets folder paths, and configures things like default materializations. profiles.yml is a separate file (by default in ~/.dbt/) that holds the actual warehouse connection details and credentials, organized into targets like dev and prod. dbt_project.yml only references a profile by name; profiles.yml resolves it into a real connection.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The key point to stress is the separation of config (in git) from secrets (outside git), and that one project can run in many environments by switching targets.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the main folders in a dbt project and what does each hold?
beginnerQuestions.answer: models/ holds SQL transformations (usually split into staging, intermediate, and marts); seeds/ holds small CSVs loaded as tables; macros/ holds reusable Jinja/SQL; tests/ holds custom singular tests; snapshots/ captures slowly changing dimensions; and analyses/ holds ad-hoc SQL that dbt compiles but does not run. Generated output goes to target/ and installed packages to dbt_packages/.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Mentioning the staging/intermediate/marts split inside models/ shows you know the recommended layering, not just the top-level folders.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you configure all staging models to be views without editing each model?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Set folder-scoped config in dbt_project.yml under the models: key: 'models: <project_name>: staging: +materialized: view'. That applies to every model in models/staging/. A model can still override it with its own config(materialized=...) block, because the most specific config wins.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show that you know the nested key must match the project name and that in-file config() overrides folder config - both are common gotchas.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is packages.yml and what does dbt deps do?
intermediateQuestions.answer: packages.yml declares third-party dbt packages (from the dbt Package Hub, git, or local paths), such as dbt-labs/dbt_utils with a pinned version. Running dbt deps downloads those packages into the dbt_packages/ directory so their macros, models, and tests are available to your project. You run dbt deps whenever packages.yml changes and typically in CI before dbt build.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize pinning versions for reproducibility and that dbt_packages/ is generated (gitignored), regenerated by dbt deps.

advancedQuestions.question: What is in the target/ directory and how are those artifacts used?
advancedQuestions.answer: target/ holds generated output: compiled SQL for each model (compiled/ and run/), manifest.json (the full parsed graph of nodes, config, and dependencies), and run_results.json (the outcome, status, and timing of the last invocation). These power dbt docs and lineage, feed monitoring, and enable state-based selection - comparing the current manifest.json to a previous one so 'dbt build --select state:modified+' rebuilds only what changed.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connecting manifest.json to state comparison and CI slim builds demonstrates production-level understanding beyond just 'it's compiled SQL'.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you manage secrets and multiple environments securely in a dbt setup?
advancedQuestions.answer: Keep profiles.yml out of git and define separate targets (dev, prod, ci) each with its own schema and role. Reference credentials with env_var() so they are injected at run time from a secrets manager rather than stored in the file. Developers default to a personal dev schema, CI builds into an ephemeral schema, and production is published only through CI using the prod target with a least-privilege role.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mentioning env_var(), least-privilege roles, and isolated schemas per target shows you understand both security and safe environment separation.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A new engineer clones your dbt repo, runs 'dbt run', and immediately gets 'Could not find profile named analytics' followed later by 'macro dbt_utils.star not found'. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Two independent setup problems. The profile error means there is no matching entry in their local profiles.yml - it is not in the repo by design, so they never created it. The dbt_utils error means packages were never installed because dbt deps was not run after cloning. Both are standard first-clone setup steps.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Have them create ~/.dbt/profiles.yml with an 'analytics' profile whose targets match dbt_project.yml (sourcing secrets from env vars), then run 'dbt debug' to confirm the connection. Then run 'dbt deps' to install dbt_utils into dbt_packages/. After that, 'dbt run' works. Document these steps in the README so every new clone knows to set up profiles.yml and run dbt deps.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a dbt project setup for a growing team that needs safe parallel development, secure secrets, reusable logic, and reproducible production builds on Snowflake.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Scaffold with dbt init; keep dbt_project.yml in git with folder-scoped materializations (staging=view, intermediate=ephemeral, marts=table) and the layered folder structure. Define profiles.yml (outside git) with dev, ci, and prod targets, each with its own schema/role and env-var credentials. Declare pinned packages in packages.yml and install with dbt deps in CI. Publish prod only through CI running 'dbt build --target prod'.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: The structured layout and multi-target setup add upfront effort and a learning curve, but they buy safety, portability, and reuse. Folder-scoped config trades a little indirection for far less boilerplate. Pinning packages trades staying-on-latest for reproducibility.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Raise threads on the prod target as model count grows, use state comparison against a stored manifest.json for slim CI builds (state:modified+), split the project into well-named domains, and share internal logic through a private package installed via packages.yml.

When would you use a seed instead of a source or a model?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A dbt project is a conventionally structured, git-tracked folder governed by dbt_project.yml, connected to a warehouse via a separate profiles.yml, with packages installed by dbt deps and compiled artifacts written to target/.
keyConcepts: dbt_project.yml (in git) names the project and configures folders/materializations; profiles.yml (outside git) holds connection secrets.
profiles.yml defines targets (dev/prod) with warehouse, schema, threads, and credentials, selected with --target.
Standard folders: models/ (staging/intermediate/marts), seeds/, macros/, tests/, snapshots/, analyses/.
packages.yml + dbt deps install reusable packages (e.g., dbt_utils) into dbt_packages/.
target/ holds generated output: manifest.json (parsed graph) and run_results.json (run outcomes) - gitignore it.
commands: dbt init analytics        # scaffold a new project + folders + dbt_project.yml
dbt deps                  # install packages from packages.yml into dbt_packages/
dbt debug                 # verify the profiles.yml connection to the warehouse
dbt compile               # resolve Jinja and write compiled SQL to target/
dbt build --target prod   # run models + tests using the prod target
interviewPoints: Config (dbt_project.yml, in git) vs secrets (profiles.yml, outside git).
Profiles have targets (dev/prod); selecting the target chooses the environment.
Folder-scoped materialization config removes per-model boilerplate; in-file config() overrides it.
packages.yml + dbt deps enable reuse (dbt_utils); pin versions for reproducibility.
target/ artifacts (manifest.json, run_results.json) power docs, monitoring, and state selection.
quickNotes: The nested key under models: must equal the project 'name'.
Gitignore target/ and dbt_packages/ - they are regenerated output.
Use env_var() in profiles.yml so credentials never live in files or git.
threads in profiles.yml controls how many models build in parallel.
Layer models as staging (stg_) -> intermediate (int_) -> marts (fct_/dim_).

keyTakeaways: A dbt project is a convention-driven folder governed by dbt_project.yml, which names the project, selects a profile, sets paths, and configures materializations per folder so conventions are enforced without per-model boilerplate.

Connection details and secrets live in a separate profiles.yml (outside git) organized into targets like dev and prod, so the same code runs safely in multiple environments just by switching --target - and credentials never enter version control.

The standard layout separates models/ (staging -> intermediate -> marts), seeds/, macros/, tests/, snapshots/, and analyses/ by responsibility, keeping large projects understandable and collaborative.
packages.yml plus dbt deps let you install and reuse community code like dbt_utils into dbt_packages/, with pinned versions for reproducible builds.

Every run compiles the project into target/, emitting manifest.json (the full parsed graph) and run_results.json (execution outcomes); these artifacts power docs, monitoring, and state-based selection, and should be gitignored as generated output.
